narrative: In the 2020s, Black and African women's hairstyles continued to thrive as a powerful expression of identity and culture. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s and resurged in popularity in the 2000s, remained a driving force behind the celebration of Afro-textured hair. Styles such as afros, cornrows, and box braids were (and remain) staples of Black beauty, with each serving as a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Africa and the African diaspora. Dreadlocks and locs also maintained their significance, allowing individuals to express themselves authentically while minimizing manipulation and exposure to environmental elements. Bantu knots, which showcase kinky hair's unique texture and density, were (and continue to be) a popular choice among those with this hair type. As protective hairstyles, these styles not only promote hair health but also serve as a declaration of self-love and pride in one's roots. While documentation from the 2020s is limited, it is clear that Black and African women's hairstyles remain an integral part of their identity and culture, celebrating the beauty and diversity of Afro-textured hair.
